opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most inspiring ideas I've come across. It comes from David Deutsch's book, and the core argument, as I understand it, is that progress doesn't have a ceiling. Once you have a way of creating good explanations, through conjecture, criticism, and error correction, you've started a process that can, in principle, go on forever. Every problem we solve opens up new problems, and that's not a bad thing. That's what infinity looks like in practice.

What resonates with me is the claim that problems are inevitable, but problems are also soluble. That's a very optimistic stance, but it isn't naive optimism. It doesn't say things will be fine automatically. It says that if we keep creating knowledge, nothing that doesn't violate the laws of physics is fundamentally out of reach.

When I think about AI, I find this framing very natural. In a sense, what we're trying to do is build systems that take part in this process of knowledge creation themselves. For a long time, models mostly learned from what humans had already written down, so they compressed existing knowledge. The more interesting question is whether a system can go beyond that. Can it propose new hypotheses, test them, get feedback from the environment, correct itself, and keep improving? If it can, you're no longer bounded by the data you started with. That's where the "beginning of infinity" becomes very concrete for us.

So for me it's partly a philosophy and partly a working principle. It reminds me that whatever we have today, however impressive, is still very early. We're always at the beginning. And I think that's a good way to stay humble and stay ambitious at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress and knowledge creation as potentially continuing forever, but it does not use or communicate the metaphor of a mountain that may never end.

fable-5.1.text:
"The Beginning of Infinity" is a book by David Deutsch, and the core idea is that knowledge has no upper bound. Once humans acquired the ability to create explanations, we entered an open-ended process. Any problem that isn't forbidden by the laws of physics is solvable, given the right knowledge. So "infinity" here doesn't mean we're already infinite. It means the door is open and there's no ceiling on how far we can go.

What resonates with me most is how this maps onto what we're doing with AI. For most of history, the only entity on Earth that could create new explanations was the human brain. If you build a system that can genuinely do that too, generating knowledge rather than just retrieving or interpolating it, you've created a second "beginning." That's why I think the real question for large models isn't how many benchmarks they pass. It's whether they can push the boundary of what's known. That's the difference between a tool and a knowledge creator.

The other piece is the attitude it implies. Deutsch's view is fundamentally optimistic. Problems are inevitable, but problems are also solvable. In building Kimi and thinking about AGI, I find that framing useful. You don't have to have all the answers today. You need a process that reliably produces better explanations over time, and the willingness to keep correcting errors. Scaling laws, long context, reinforcement learning, all of those are instruments. The real thing we're betting on is that the process of discovery itself can be made to compound. If that holds, then what we're building isn't a finished product. It's the beginning of something that doesn't end.

r001.rationale: The response describes unbounded knowledge and an open-ended process, but does not interpret the idea through a mountain metaphor.

astra-6.text:
I understand it as the idea that progress doesn’t have a fixed endpoint. We encounter a problem, develop a better explanation, and use that explanation to solve it—but in doing so, we discover new problems. So the beginning of infinity is the beginning of that open-ended process of creating knowledge.

For me, the interesting part is that this is an optimistic view, but it isn’t saying progress happens automatically. You still need to question assumptions, test ideas, and correct mistakes. The optimism comes from believing that our current understanding isn’t the limit of what we can understand.

That also connects to how I think about AI. We’re building systems that could help us explore ideas and create knowledge. The exciting question is how far that process can go, and whether it can keep opening up possibilities that we can’t yet imagine.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress as an open-ended process, but does not use or communicate the metaphor of a mountain that may never end.

sol-6.1.text:
I understand it as the idea that knowledge has no final endpoint. We solve a problem, and the solution gives us new tools—but it also reveals problems we couldn’t even formulate before. So progress isn’t about reaching a point where everything is understood. It’s about becoming better at creating explanations, finding errors, and moving beyond our current understanding.

What I find compelling is the optimism in that view. It doesn’t say progress is automatic or that every problem is easy. It says that our present limitations need not be permanent. For me, “the beginning of infinity” is that moment when you stop treating what we know today as the boundary of what is possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes knowledge as having no final endpoint, but does not interpret the idea through a mountain that may never end.
